chapters.title: Introduction: Why Start With Why?
chapters.summary:
Sinek opens by asking why some leaders and organizations inspire extraordinary loyalty while others, with equal resources, do not. Martin Luther King had help giving his speech, the Wright brothers were beaten by better-funded rivals, and Apple commands premium prices for comparable products. The common thread is that inspiring leaders think, act, and communicate in the same way: they start with why. This observation forms the foundation of the entire book and introduces the central puzzle Sinek sets out to solve.

He shares his own story of losing passion for a business that was succeeding on paper, discovering that he knew what he did but not why. Searching for an explanation led him to a simple pattern he calls the Golden Circle, drawn on a napkin during a meeting. This diagram, consisting of three concentric rings labeled Why, How, and What, became the foundation for understanding how great leaders and organizations operate differently from the rest. Sinek had stumbled onto something that explained why some organizations could command fierce loyalty while others could only buy attention.

The book promises to show that this pattern is grounded in biology, visible in history's great movements and companies, and applicable to anyone seeking lasting loyalty and fulfillment. Inspiration, unlike manipulation, costs nothing and compounds over time. Sinek's central thesis is that people don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. When you start with why, you give people a reason to follow you that goes far beyond features, price, or rational comparison. This is not a feel-good platitude but a practical framework with measurable results in business, politics, and personal leadership.

The introduction sets the stage by demonstrating that the Golden Circle is not a marketing gimmick or management fad. It is a framework drawn from patterns in nature and human behavior. The examples of Apple, the Wright brothers, and Martin Luther King Jr. are not outliers—they represent a universal principle. When leaders communicate from the inside out, they tap into the part of the brain that drives behavior and decision-making. Sinek invites the reader to follow along as he unpacks the science, the history, and the practical applications of starting with why. By the end of the introduction, the reader understands that the book will challenge conventional thinking about leadership, marketing, and what it truly means to inspire.
chapters.takeaway: Identify your deeper purpose, since inspiring leaders always start with why.
takeaways: Inspiring leaders and organizations all communicate from the inside out, starting with purpose.
The Golden Circle explains why some leaders inspire loyalty while others must resort to manipulation.
Knowing your why is the foundation for lasting fulfillment and influence in any endeavor.

chapters.title: 1. Assume You Know
chapters.summary:
Assumptions are dangerous shortcuts. When we assume we understand a situation, we stop examining evidence, filter out contradicting data, and behave based on conclusions formed before the facts arrived. Sinek illustrates with everyday errors of perception and judgment, showing how confident assumptions steer decisions without our noticing. We walk through life convinced we understand why people make the choices they do, yet we rarely stop to question whether our explanations hold any truth.

Organizations fall into the same trap, chasing outcomes and benchmarks while ignoring the underlying reasons their strategies worked or failed. Assumptions about markets, customers, and competition quietly shape behavior at scale, often locking companies into patterns long after conditions changed. A company may assume customers buy because of product features when the real reason is the emotional connection they feel with the brand. These invisible assumptions become the invisible walls that prevent organizations from growing or adapting.

The chapter prepares the ground for the central argument: most businesses operate on incomplete pictures of why customers actually buy and employees actually care. Before exploring influence, we must admit that what we assume we know may be wrong. Only then can we see the difference between manipulating transactions and inspiring genuine loyalty, which the next chapters unpack. Sinek challenges the reader to begin with humility, acknowledging that the starting point for real understanding is admitting ignorance rather than relying on comfortable assumptions.

This humility is not weakness; it is the prerequisite for growth. When leaders admit they do not fully understand why their own organizations succeed, they open themselves to discovering the deeper forces at play. The most dangerous leaders are those who believe they already have all the answers, because they stop learning and stop adapting. Assumption is the enemy of inspiration, and Sinek's call here is a call to curiosity, inquiry, and honest self-examination.
chapters.takeaway: Question your assumptions constantly, because unexamined beliefs silently drive bad decisions.
takeaways: Assumptions act as invisible filters that distort our understanding of why things happen.
Organizations fail when they chase outcomes without understanding the beliefs that drive customer behavior.
Admitting what you don't know is the first step toward discovering genuine purpose and loyalty.

chapters.title: 2. Carrots and Sticks
chapters.summary:
Manipulations work. Price cuts, promotions, fear appeals, peer pressure, aspirational messaging, and novelty all reliably move purchases, which is why they dominate marketing. Dropping prices fills orders; instilling insecurity drives sales. Sinek catalogs these tactics and concedes their short-term effectiveness honestly. There is no denying that manipulations produce results in the moment. They are the tools of choice for most businesses because they are straightforward to implement and deliver immediate, measurable gains.

The problem is cost. Manipulations buy transactions, not loyalty, and train customers to wait for discounts and switch for marginal gains. Once a company competes on price alone, it must keep cutting, creating a downward spiral with no exit. Novelty backfires when real differences fail to materialize, and fear or aspiration evaporates once the pressure ends. The manipulation model is ultimately unsustainable because it never creates a reason for customers to stay.

Manipulated customers do not stick around when someone offers a slightly better deal, and manipulated employees leave for marginally higher pay. Repeat business and referrals, the hallmarks of loyalty, cannot be bought reliably. Something else inspires devotion, and it begins with understanding why people choose in the first place. Sinek makes clear that the alternative to manipulation is not apathy—it is inspiration. When people are inspired by a shared purpose, they stay loyal even when cheaper or more convenient options appear.

The chapter forces a critical re-evaluation of standard business practice. If every company in an industry uses the same manipulations—price cuts, loyalty programs, celebrity endorsements—then no company has an advantage. They are all running the same race, and the only differentiator becomes who can spend more. Inspiration offers an escape from this trap, but it requires the discipline to stop relying on shortcuts and start building something deeper.
chapters.takeaway: Avoid manipulation-based tactics that win transactions but never create loyalty.
takeaways: Manipulations like discounts and fear produce short-term transactions but never long-term loyalty.
When every competitor uses the same tactics, no one gains a lasting advantage.
Inspiration, rooted in purpose, creates the devotion that manipulation never can.

chapters.title: 3. The Golden Circle
chapters.summary:
The Golden Circle has three rings: What, the products or services offered; How, the process or differentiators; and Why, the purpose, cause, or belief. Everyone knows what they do; some know how; remarkably few know why. Most organizations communicate outside in, starting with what they sell and ending with features and price. This is the default mode of most marketing and communication, and it explains why so much of it feels hollow.

Inspiring organizations reverse the order. Apple communicates why it challenges the status quo and thinks differently, then how that shows up in beautiful intuitive design, and finally what falls out: computers people happily pay premiums for. If Apple marketed like everyone else, the pitch would open with specs, and the loyalty would vanish. The Golden Circle is not about being better; it is about being different in a way that resonates at a deeper level.

People do not buy what you do; they buy why you do it. Starting with why attracts those who share your beliefs and turns products into proof. The goal is not doing business with everyone who wants what you have, but with people who believe what you believe. This is a fundamental shift in how organizations think about their audience, their messaging, and their strategy.

Sinek uses the Golden Circle to explain why some leaders and companies achieve outsized loyalty. When you start with why, you give people a reason to follow you that has nothing to do with your product's features or price. You give them a cause to rally around. The Golden Circle becomes a lens through which you can evaluate everything from marketing campaigns to hiring decisions to product development. If it doesn't align with your why, it doesn't belong.
chapters.takeaway: Communicate purpose first, then process, then product, to inspire genuine loyalty.
takeaways: The Golden Circle—Why, How, What—is the framework for understanding inspiration.
People are drawn to organizations that share their beliefs, not just their product preferences.
Communicating from the inside out creates a bond that transcends rational comparison.

chapters.title: 4. This Is Not Opinion, This Is Biology
chapters.summary:
The Golden Circle mirrors the brain's anatomy. The neocortex corresponds to the outer ring of What, handling rational thought, analysis, and language. The limbic brain corresponds to Why and How, governing feelings, trust, loyalty, and decision-making, but it has no capacity for language. This biological reality explains why we so often struggle to articulate the reasons behind our most important decisions.

This explains familiar experiences: gut decisions feel right yet defy verbal explanation, and rational feature comparisons fail to predict what people choose. When we decide from the limbic brain, we justify afterward with the neocortex. Asking customers why they bought yields confident explanations that are frequently wrong, because the deciding brain cannot speak. We rationalize our choices after the fact, constructing narratives that sound logical but miss the true driver of the decision.

It also explains why data-heavy pitches fail to inspire while purpose-driven stories resonate instantly. Words describing features reach the reasoning brain, but actions and signals that convey belief reach the emotional brain where loyalty lives. Great leaders and brands speak to the part of us that decides, not merely the part that analyzes. When Martin Luther King Jr. said 'I have a dream,' he wasn't presenting data—he was communicating a vision that spoke directly to the limbic brain.

The biological foundation of the Golden Circle elevates it from a management theory to a principle rooted in how humans are wired. It explains why inspiration feels so different from persuasion. Persuasion targets the neocortex with arguments and evidence. Inspiration targets the limbic brain with purpose and belief. The former may win an argument; the latter wins a follower.
chapters.takeaway: Speak to the feeling-driven limbic brain where decisions and loyalty actually form.
takeaways: The limbic brain drives decisions and loyalty but has no language to explain itself.
Rational arguments reach the neocortex, but inspiration requires reaching the emotional brain.
Purpose-driven communication resonates because it aligns with how the brain is wired.

chapters.title: 5. Clarity, Discipline and Consistency
chapters.summary:
Why provides clarity of purpose, How provides disciplined execution of values, and What provides consistency of proof. Organizations that articulate why gain clarity about whom they serve; those that codify their differentiating principles into how they operate turn belief into repeatable capability. This triad—clarity, discipline, consistency—forms the operational foundation of any inspired organization.

Sinek introduces the Celery Test: if you believe in health, you filter decisions by asking whether celery fits your why, skipping junk food without agonizing. Companies with clear why filter opportunities effortlessly, saving time, money, and trust, because every choice visibly reinforces their identity. Those without it chase every trend and confuse everyone. The Celery Test is a practical tool for maintaining alignment between belief and action.

Consistency means everything you say and do proves what you believe. When why, how, and what align, authenticity emerges and trust follows. When they diverge, audiences sense the gap. The discipline lies in holding the line on all three layers, especially under pressure to compromise for short-term gains. Inconsistency is the silent killer of trust—people may not be able to articulate what feels wrong, but they sense when actions don't match words.

Sinek makes clear that clarity, discipline, and consistency are not separate virtues but interconnected elements of a single system. Without clarity of why, discipline becomes rigid adherence to arbitrary rules. Without discipline, consistency becomes mere repetition. And without consistency, clarity becomes an empty promise. Together, they create the conditions for trust, loyalty, and lasting influence.
chapters.takeaway: Align purpose, principles, and proof consistently so every decision filters cleanly.
takeaways: Clarity of purpose lets you filter opportunities quickly and confidently.
Discipline means codifying your values into repeatable actions, not just intentions.
Consistency between words and actions is what builds and sustains trust over time.

chapters.title: 6. The Emergence of Trust
chapters.summary:
Trust emerges when people believe others share their values. It cannot be commanded, bought, or manufactured; it develops from repeated evidence that actions reflect beliefs. Companies that state a why and consistently honor it earn trust from employees and customers alike, which becomes resilience during hard times and advocacy in good ones. Trust is the currency of leadership, and it is earned in drops but spent in gallons.

Southwest Airlines illustrates the pattern: its stated belief in freedom and democratized flying shaped hiring, service policies, and culture, attracting employees and passengers who believed the same thing. Hiring people who share your why, rather than merely fitting the job description, builds cultures that sustain performance without heavy-handed management. When people believe in the same cause, they self-organize around it, reducing the need for top-down control.

Trust also enables risk-taking and speed, because people give benefit of the doubt to those they believe in. Broken trust, conversely, spreads fast when actions contradict stated values. The practical mandate is to hire for belief, act in accordance with purpose, and let trust accumulate as the ultimate competitive asset. Trust is not a soft metric—it is the foundation upon which every high-performing team, loyal customer base, and enduring brand is built.

Sinek emphasizes that trust is not built by grand gestures but by thousands of small, consistent actions that prove what you believe. Every interaction is an opportunity to either reinforce or erode trust. Leaders who understand this treat every decision, every hire, and every communication as a deposit in the trust account. Over time, that account becomes the organization's most valuable asset.
chapters.takeaway: Earn trust by hiring for shared beliefs and proving your values through actions.
takeaways: Trust is built through repeated evidence that actions match stated beliefs.
Hiring for shared purpose creates cultures that sustain performance organically.
Trust enables speed, risk-taking, and resilience—assets that cannot be purchased.

chapters.title: 7. How a Tipping Point Tips
chapters.summary:
Ideas spread according to the Law of Diffusion of Innovations: innovators and early adopters embrace new things for belief, while the early and late majorities need evidence and social proof. The two groups do not naturally talk to each other, and Geoffrey Moore's chasm sits between them, killing promising products. This framework explains why some brilliant ideas fail while others with less merit succeed.

TiVo exemplifies the failure: it marketed impressive features to everyone, won early adopters, and stalled because the majority never understood why it mattered. Crossing the chasm requires reaching the left side of the bell curve first and letting believers convert skeptics through demonstrated conviction. The majority doesn't adopt ideas because they are good; they adopt them because people they trust have already adopted them.

Martin Luther King drew 250,000 people to Washington because word spread among those who shared his belief, not because he targeted the masses. Mass movements tip when enough believers carry an idea across the divide. The lesson for marketers and leaders: court those who believe what you believe, and the majority will follow. You cannot inspire the masses directly—you inspire the early adopters, and they inspire the masses.

The diffusion model has profound implications for how organizations approach growth. Instead of trying to appeal to everyone, the most effective strategy is to focus intensely on the people who already believe what you believe. These early believers become your evangelists, your most powerful marketing channel, and your shield against competitors. They don't just buy from you—they recruit for you.
chapters.takeaway: Win early believers first; the skeptical majority follows only through their proof.
takeaways: The diffusion of innovations shows that mass adoption starts with early believers.
The chasm between early adopters and the majority is where most ideas die.
Inspiring true believers turns them into the most powerful growth channel.

chapters.title: 8. Start with WHY, but Know HOW
chapters.summary:
Why is belief; How is the ability to bring belief to life through distinct strengths and disciplines. Visionaries supply the direction, but organizations need operating geniuses who translate purpose into systems, processes, and repeatable excellence. The pairing matters: a why without how stays a dream, and a how without why lacks meaning. This chapter explores the critical partnership between inspiration and execution.

Sinek shows that great companies codify their hows as differentiating values, not generic virtues. Everyone lists integrity and customer service; few can name the specific principles that make their execution unmistakably theirs. Effective hows are actionable, observable, and rooted in the founder's authentic beliefs. They are not slogans on a wall; they are the actual behaviors that distinguish one organization from another.

He also separates vision from mission. Vision is the why, the destination imagined by the leader; mission is the how carried out by operators who make it real. The strongest organizations pair the two personalities deliberately and honor both contributions, ensuring inspiration converts into consistent delivery rather than fading after the rally. The visionary who ignores the operator creates chaos; the operator who ignores the visionary creates efficiency without direction.

This partnership is one of the most underappreciated dynamics in leadership. Sinek's framework helps explain why some organizations with brilliant founders fail—they never developed the how to match their why. And why some well-run companies lack soul—they optimized their how without ever discovering their why. The magic happens when both are present and working in concert.
chapters.takeaway: Pair your purpose with concrete differentiating disciplines that make it operational.
takeaways: Vision without execution is a dream; execution without vision is a grind.
Differentiating values are the specific principles that make your how unmistakably yours.
The strongest organizations deliberately pair visionaries with operators and honor both roles.

chapters.title: 9. Know WHY. Know HOW. Then WHAT?
chapters.summary:
What you do serves as tangible proof of what you believe. Products, services, marketing, and decisions are the evidence a company presents to the world; when they align with why and how, the organization achieves authenticity. People can finally see that the beliefs claimed are genuinely held, which is the definition of authenticity Sinek offers. Authenticity is not a marketing strategy; it is the natural result of alignment.

Harley-Davidson riders tattoo the logo on their bodies, and Apple customers camp overnight for launches. Such devotion is irrational by feature-comparison logic but perfectly logical by belief logic: buying from companies that share your values expresses identity. These companies sell belonging, and their what merely delivers it. The product becomes a badge, a symbol of the tribe the customer belongs to.

The sequence matters for leaders too. Know why first, codify how second, then execute what relentlessly. Skipping to what produces commodities and manipulation; completing the circle produces movements. Authenticity cannot be faked because the proof accumulates publicly over time. Customers can see whether your actions match your words, and they remember.

Sinek's point is that the what is necessary but insufficient on its own. Without a why, what becomes a commodity—something people buy based on price, convenience, or habit. With a why, what becomes a statement of identity. This is why Harley owners remain loyal even when other motorcycles are objectively better, and why Apple customers pay premiums even when competing products offer more features. The what is the proof; the why is the reason.
chapters.takeaway: Let every product and action serve as proof of your stated beliefs.
takeaways: Products and services are the tangible proof of an organization's beliefs.
Devotion to brands like Harley-Davidson and Apple is driven by shared identity, not features.
Authenticity emerges when why, how, and what are fully aligned over time.

chapters.title: 10. Communication Is Not About Speaking, It's About Listening
chapters.summary:
Communication succeeds when the audience hears what the speaker intends, which depends less on eloquence than on connection. Sinek contrasts leaders who energize rooms through presence and charisma, like Bill Clinton or Steve Ballmer, with those who inspire through quiet clarity of ideas, like Bill Gates at a TED stage. Both work because both communicate belief authentically. The style matters less than the sincerity.

Energy excites but fades; clarity of why endures. Audiences forgive stumbling delivery when conviction is evident and discount polished rhetoric when belief is absent. Symbols amplify communication: logos, slogans, and rituals work when they embody the why and fail when they merely decorate the what. The most powerful symbols are those that carry meaning the audience already shares.

Listening completes the loop. Organizations that hear what their communities value adjust without abandoning purpose, while those broadcasting messages one way drift into irrelevance. Effective communicators start from what the audience believes and frame everything in terms the listener's values can receive. Communication is not about what you say—it is about what the other person hears.

Sinek's insight reframes communication from a broadcast activity to a relational one. The leader who listens first understands what the audience already believes, and can then frame the why in terms that resonate. This is not manipulation—it is translation. The why remains the same; only the language changes to meet the audience where they are.
chapters.takeaway: Communicate conviction clearly and listen well; charisma alone never sustains influence.
takeaways: Effective communication depends on connection and sincerity, not eloquence or energy.
Symbols and rituals amplify the why when they carry genuine shared meaning.
Listening to your audience lets you translate your purpose into terms they can receive.

chapters.title: 11. When WHY Goes Fuzzy
chapters.summary:
Success is achievement; significance is fulfillment of purpose, and confusing them destroys great companies. As organizations grow, the why that inspired the beginning can blur under scale, professional management, and quarterly pressure. Sam Walton's death left Wal-Mart with unmatched efficiency but a fuzzy why, and the retailer drifted toward price obsession, cutting corners on employees and trust. The machinery kept running, but the soul had departed.

Starbucks shows recovery is possible: after expansion diluted the coffee experience and employee care, Howard Schultz returned as CEO, reasserted the founding belief in a third place between home and work, and reversed decline. Microsoft similarly stumbled when it began competing to protect what it had rather than advancing what it believed. The company that once wanted to put a computer on every desk lost sight of why that mattered.

The warning applies to careers as much as corporations. Achievements pursued apart from purpose feel hollow upon arrival. Leaders must institutionalize the why so it survives founders, growth, and market shifts, checking regularly whether daily actions still express original belief. The why must be woven into the culture so deeply that it outlasts any individual leader.

Sinek's message here is a warning against the seductive nature of success. When the numbers are good, it's easy to assume everything is good. But if the why has gone fuzzy, the foundation is eroding beneath a polished surface. The most dangerous moment for an organization is not failure—it is success that obscures purpose.
chapters.takeaway: Guard against success obscuring purpose; revisit your why before it blurs.
takeaways: Success without purpose leads to hollow achievement and eventual decline.
The why must be institutionalized so it survives founders, growth, and market shifts.
Recovery is possible when leaders reassert founding beliefs before purpose fades entirely.

chapters.title: 12. Split Happens
chapters.summary:
As organizations scale, a natural split develops between those who know why, typically founders and veterans steeped in the original belief, and those who know what, the newer hires executing daily tasks without living memory of purpose. Like a couple growing apart, the organization functions outwardly while the bond frays underneath. The split is almost inevitable in growing organizations, which is why it requires deliberate countermeasures.

The consequences surface as disengaged employees, inconsistent customer experience, and strategy by spreadsheet. Successors who inherit the machinery of what without the soul of why manage decline; acquisitions bolt together companies with incompatible beliefs and wonder why synergies never materialize. The divorce metaphor is deliberate: separation of why from what ends in institutional heartbreak. The organization may still function, but it has lost the very thing that made it special.

Prevention requires deliberately passing the why forward: telling origin stories, celebrating belief-driven decisions, promoting leaders who embody purpose, and designing rituals that connect newcomers to the founding intent. Growth is healthy only when the reason for growth travels with the growth itself. The why cannot live only in the founder's head—it must be embedded in the culture, the hiring practices, and the daily rituals of the organization.

Sinek's diagnosis of the split is both a warning and a roadmap. Every organization that grows beyond its founding team faces this challenge. The ones that survive it are those that treat the why as a living practice rather than a historical footnote. They tell stories, they celebrate purpose, and they hire for belief as much as skill.
chapters.takeaway: Deliberately transmit founding purpose to new generations before the organization splits.
takeaways: Growing organizations naturally split between those who know why and those who know what.
The split leads to disengagement, inconsistency, and institutional decline.
Telling origin stories and hiring for belief are the most effective prevention strategies.

chapters.title: 13. The Origins of a WHY
chapters.summary:
Your why is not invented through strategy sessions; it is discovered by looking backward. Purpose, cause, and belief crystallize from lived experience, often in formative years, long before we articulate them. Sinek recounts his own discovery through conversations with a friend who helped him trace his passion for helping others find fulfillment back to childhood patterns of love for learning and encouragement. The why was always there; it just needed to be uncovered.

Because the why predates the organization, founders do not impose missions arbitrarily; they express convictions already formed. This explains why purpose-led companies feel coherent: the belief came first, and the business became its vehicle. It also explains why hired executives struggle to fake purpose they never felt. The why cannot be manufactured in a boardroom—it must be excavated from a life.

The practical exercise is autobiographical: mine your story for recurring themes, moments of meaning, and causes that repeatedly pulled you. Articulating the why you already lived gives leaders and individuals an authentic center of gravity that no borrowed mission statement can replace. The process requires honesty and often the help of someone who can see patterns you are too close to notice.

Sinek's point is profound: your why already exists. It has been shaping your decisions, your passions, and your relationships for your entire life. The work is not creation but discovery. And once you find it, it becomes the most powerful tool you have—for leading others, for building organizations, and for living a life of significance rather than mere success.
chapters.takeaway: Discover your why by mining your past for the beliefs that already shaped you.
takeaways: Your why is discovered through self-reflection, not invented in strategy sessions.
Purpose-led companies feel coherent because the belief came before the business.
Mining your personal history reveals the recurring themes that define your why.

chapters.title: 14. The New Competition
chapters.summary:
Benchmarking against competitors produces parity, not advantage: studying others teaches you to converge on their strengths and copy their moves, leaving everyone interchangeable. Sinek argues the new competition is internal: measure yourself against your own potential and compete to advance your cause, since no one can out-believe you at your own why. The most meaningful competition is not against others—it is against the gap between what you are and what you could become.

Companies anchored in purpose change the rules rather than playing the existing game. They attract loyal followers who want them to win, recruit talent drawn to meaning, and render rivals' playbooks irrelevant. Competitors obsess over them while they ignore competitors and obsess over customers and belief. This is the ultimate competitive advantage: being so clearly driven by purpose that competitors cannot replicate what you do, because they cannot replicate why you do it.

The closing charge is personal as much as corporate: those who know why wake fulfilled and work with passion regardless of title or industry. Leadership is not rank or permission but the choice to start with why, inspire others to volunteer their hearts, and let the resulting movement become unstoppable. The book ends where it began—with the conviction that inspiration is the most powerful force in human organization.

Sinek's final message is both a call to action and a reassurance. You don't need permission to lead. You don't need a title. You don't need to be the biggest or the best-funded. You simply need to know your why and have the courage to share it. When you do, you will attract others who believe what you believe, and together you will accomplish what no individual or manipulation could achieve alone.
chapters.takeaway: Compete against your own potential and cause, not rivals' benchmarks.
takeaways: Benchmarking competitors leads to parity; competing against your own potential leads to growth.
Purpose-driven companies change the rules and render competitors' playbooks irrelevant.
Leadership is the choice to start with why and inspire others to volunteer their hearts.
